title: Mother speaks for self, son at coroner's inquest
article: In the line of suits along the bar at the Kevin St. Arnaud coroner's inquest, there is one in department store attire.
She looks more like a mother than a lawyer, and she is. Dolores Young and her husband Brian chose to represent themselves at the probe into the death of their son.

To Young's right is the lawyer representing Rebecca Gingera, St. Arnaud's common law wife. To her immediate left is the legal counsel for the RCMP. Farther to her left is the lawyer for the B.C. Coroner's Service. Before them all sits Regional Coroner Shane De Meyer.
In the legal crossfire Young rises to speak infrequently and in blunt sentences that insist there be no assassination of her son's character.
"I just feel I have to protect Kevin," Young told the Citizen. "I think it is important to have a second voice up there."

She and Brian knew Gingera had lawyer Cameron Ward in their corner and felt confident Ward would get to the heart of the police shooting that killed St. Arnaud, then 29. According to preliminary testimony, on Dec. 19, 2004 at about 1 a.m. Vanderhoof RCMP responded to an intruder alarm at a drugstore and saw St. Arnaud run from the rear of the building.

After a foot chase through the snow across a tennis court and onto a soccer pitch, St. Arnaud apparently turned to face his pursuers. Const. Ryan Sherematta, fearing for his life, then fired three bullets that all struck potentially lethal wounds. St. Arnaud was pronounced dead within minutes.

"I don't think any good can come of this," said Brian, who sits behind Young in the front row of the public gallery, his face perpetually vexed. "They've all made up their minds about how it's going to go. I mean they have already decided they aren't going to pursue charges. I just wish the officer wasn't getting off so scot- free."
Provincial Crown counsel announced in February, 2006 that the internal RCMP investigation of the matter was done and the evidence did not support charges against Sherematta.
It was then the coroner's inquest was announced. Although it is shaped somewhat like a trial, though, it does not find fault with a person or institution for a death, only the root cause.
Gingera told the Citizen that she feels the spotlight has been turned onto Kevin instead of Sherematta.

"If this were a civilian who shot and killed someone he would have been in court the next day but because it was a police officer everything gets hidden from the public and we don't get to hear about who Sherematta was, we only hear about Kevin," Gingera said.

She said the public ought to know that St. Arnaud was never violent towards her or anyone else she knows of. She heard that he did some drugs in his youth but never in their life together and he rarely drank alcohol.
He was a hard worker, a fun person with a good sense of humour, and a talented artist who carved soapstone and welded metal sculptures, she said.
The inquest began Thursday and resumes Jan. 23 to 26 and Jan. 29 to 31.
